Neonatal Sika deer (Cervus nippon) fawns typically enter the world weighing approximately 5750 grams [Wwb = approximately 5750 grams], a value documented in several Hokkaido populations. This birth mass is relatively modest for a cervid of this body size and reflects the species' strategy of producing a single, well-developed offspring after a complete gestation. The suckling period, during which the fawn remains entirely dependent on its mother's milk, lasts for about 172 days after birth [tx = about 172 days after birth], a duration measured in captive herds maintained at a core body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This extended nursing phase is critical for the fawn's development, allowing it to build substantial energy reserves before the nutritional stress of winter. At the point of weaning, a healthy fawn has usually accumulated a wet weight of 28590 grams [Wwx = 28590 grams], representing a more than fourfold increase from its neonatal mass. This period of rapid mass gain is fueled entirely by maternal investment and underscores the high energetic cost of lactation for the hind, a factor that strongly influences inter-birth intervals and overall reproductive output in this species.

As female Sika deer approach the completion of their somatic growth, their ultimate wet weight stabilizes around 50,000 grams [Wwi = around 50,000 grams], whereas males continue to develop significantly larger frames, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 109,000 grams [Wwi = 109,000 grams]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in body mass, with males nearly doubling the size of females, is a hallmark of the species and is closely tied to the polygynous mating system. Heavier stags enjoy a distinct advantage during the autumn rut, where competition for access to receptive hinds favors larger body size. Females, in contrast, allocate a greater proportion of their energy budget to gestation and lactation rather than continued skeletal growth. Consequently, the growth trajectories of the two sexes diverge markedly after the first year of life, a pattern that is consistent among northern populations of the species. This divergence in adult mass profoundly shapes their respective life-history strategies, influencing everything from foraging behavior to predation risk and social dominance within mixed-sex herds.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Sika deer in the wild has been documented at roughly 9,600 days [am = roughly 9,600 days], a figure derived from long-term field studies on protected islands at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]in Japan. This estimate of longevity was obtained from individuals monitored under natural thermal conditions where core body temperature averaged 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. Such a lifespan is relatively extended for a medium-sized deer and speaks to the effectiveness of predator-avoidance behaviors and the seasonal abundance of high-quality forage in their native habitats. Old age is typically accompanied by pronounced tooth wear, which limits the efficiency of mastication and leads to a gradual decline in body condition. Senescence becomes particularly evident in females past the age of ten years, where reproductive output begins to diminish. The oldest individuals are often those that have successfully avoided predation and severe winters, benefiting from the species' inherent physiological resilience. This longevity represents a key life-history parameter that, when combined with relatively low annual fecundity, shapes the slow and steady population dynamics characteristic of many Sika deer populations.

Reproduction in Sika deer is defined by a low, steady fecundity, as hinds typically produce a single fawn per parturition [N_R_i = single fawn per parturition], and the interval between births is generally one year, yielding approximately one birth event annually [F_R_i = approximately one birth event annually]. This monovular reproductive strategy is energetically constrained; the gestation period, which is remarkably consistent at 210 days [tg = 210 days] at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], represents a substantial investment. Some field records, particularly from captive studies, indicate a slightly wider range of 249 to 253 days [tg = of 249 to 253 days], though the 210-day figure is more frequently cited for the subspecies Cervus nippon yesoensis. The combination of a singular birth and a lengthy gestation means that annual recruitment is heavily dependent on the survival of that single fawn through its first winter. This constraint drives strong maternal care behaviors and a preference for sheltered fawning sites that minimize predation risk. The low annual fecundity is offset by a relatively high survival rate among neonates that survive their first few weeks of life.

Puberty in Sika deer, defined as the age at which individuals first become capable of producing viable gametes, is reached approximately 500 days after birth [tp = approximately 500 days after birth], a developmental milestone achieved under normal thermoregulatory conditions (core body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]). This timing means that most females are capable of conceiving during their second autumn of life, though successful breeding in the first year of adulthood is contingent on attaining sufficient body condition. Males, on the other hand, often experience a social delay in actual mating success despite reaching physiological maturity at a similar age, as their smaller body size and subordinate social status prevent effective competition with older, heavier stags during the rut. The onset of puberty is tightly linked to a threshold of body mass accumulation; individuals that fail to reach a critical mass during their juvenile period will delay maturation by a full year. This plasticity in the timing of reproductive activation is a crucial adaptation to variable environmental conditions, allowing the population to forego reproduction when resources are scarce. The relationship between body condition and puberty ensures that only well-provisioned individuals contribute to the gene pool.
